deep.reconstruction:
Folio 28v carries almost no original work. The visible content is the mirror-image bleed-through of the recto (28r, transcribed as the previous page). The only ink that appears to belong to this side is a few scattered figures, roughly '5930', '615', '2084' and '2', near the top of the 2nd and 3rd columns. They are too fragmentary to interpret and may also be heavier recto ink showing through. The reconstruction below therefore concerns the recto content seen through the paper.

(A) Table. The argument runs from 0° to 180° in steps of 7°30', giving 25 values, i.e. a division of the full circle into 48 parts. There are four numerical columns, which I call F1, F2, F3, F4. At 0° they read F1 = 2.0863825, F2 = 0.5952987, F3 = 0.2899531, F4 = 1.9228841. At 180° they read F1 = 4.4208363, F2 = 1.1285758, F3 = 0.1061941, F4 = 1.2770094. F1 and F2 increase monotonically; F3 and F4 decrease. Each column is even about 0° and 180°, so it is a smooth periodic even function of an angle (presumably an anomaly or elongation). This is the typical set-up for a secular or periodic perturbation, or ring-attraction, computation.

I could not determine with certainty how F1, F2 and F3 are defined or how they combine into F4. Trial combinations, including AGM-type ones, did not reproduce F4, so that link is left open. The next page (f.29) has a parallel 48-point table with an angle near 57°41', complex values 1.684 ± 2.664 i and harmonic coefficients. Together with the marginal note ∛(1.4471580)/a, this places the sheet in a celestial-mechanics computation, possibly connected with Gauss's ring-attraction or secular-perturbation work. That attribution is my conjecture.

(B) Harmonic coefficients. The list (0) ... (24) is the cosine expansion of column F4:
 F4(θ) = Σ_{n=0}^{24} c_n cos(nθ).
Here c_0 = 1.6573844. The coefficients (1)–(14) are written in units of 10^-7: c_1 = +0.3083332, c_2 = −0.0531409, c_3 = +0.0132344, c_4 = −0.0038375, c_5 = +0.0012102, c_6 = −0.0004025, c_7 = +0.0001390, c_8 = −0.0000493, c_9 = +0.0000178, c_10 = −0.0000065, c_11 = +0.0000024, c_12 = −0.0000010, c_13 = +0.0000004, c_14 = −0.0000001. The coefficients (15)–(24) are fractions of a unit of 10^-7 (−0.71, +0.29?, +0.08, +0.06, +0.41, +0.12, −0.47, +0.04, −0.22, +0.60) and are pure rounding noise.

The 25 equidistant values determine exactly 25 cosine coefficients, the trigonometric-interpolation case. They can be obtained by
 c_0 = (1/24)·Σ' F4(θ_k),
 c_n = (1/12)·Σ' F4(θ_k) cos(nθ_k),
where Σ' halves the end terms and the last coefficient is also halved (my statement of the standard formulas). The fact that c_15 ... c_24 come out at the level of the last decimal shows that the series has effectively terminated by n ≈ 14. It thus serves both as a convergence check and as a check on the accuracy of the tabulated values. The successive ratios |c_{n+1}/c_n| rise toward about 0.37. This is geometric convergence, consistent with an analytic periodic function such as a function of a distance |1 − α e^{iθ}|.

Verification (mine):
- At θ = 0, Σ c_n = 1.9228841. The table gives 1.9228841.
- At θ = 180°, Σ (−1)^n c_n = 1.2770092. The table gives 1.2770094.
- At θ = 90°, c_0 − c_2 + c_4 − c_6 + ... = 1.7070466. The table gives 1.7070467.
So the coefficient list is the Fourier analysis of the last column.
errors: No error found in the recto work visible here: the cosine series reproduces F4 at 0°, 90° and 180° to within 1–2 units of the 7th decimal.

The noise coefficients (15)–(24) reach about 0.7·10^-7. That is somewhat larger than pure 7-decimal rounding would give (expected about 0.1–0.2·10^-7), suggesting small errors of a few units in the 7th decimal of some tabulated F4 values. This is a minor accuracy point, not a mistake in the analysis.

results.what: Tabulation of four smooth even periodic functions of an angle at 48-fold equidistant division (step 7.5°, 0°–180°).
results.modern_name: Equidistant sampling for discrete Fourier analysis
results.usually_credited_to: Standard 18th–19th c. astronomical practice (Clairaut, Lagrange, Bessel, Gauss)

results.what: Cosine (harmonic) expansion of the last column from its 25 values, giving coefficients c_0..c_24; the high-order coefficients serve as a precision and convergence check.
results.modern_name: Trigonometric interpolation / discrete cosine transform (harmonic analysis)
results.usually_credited_to: Clairaut 1754 and Lagrange; Gauss, 'Theoria interpolationis methodo nova tractata' (c.1805, publ. posthumously) including FFT-type schemes

deep.surprise_reason: The verso is essentially bleed-through. The recto material is a standard Gaussian harmonic analysis of a perturbation-type function at 48 points, a technique well documented as Gauss's (Theoria interpolationis, Pallas perturbations). It is a nice concrete worked example but not new.

checkable.asserts: The cosine series at θ=0 reproduces the tabulated F4(0)=1.9228841.
The cosine series at θ=180° reproduces F4(180°)=1.2770094.
The cosine series at θ=90° reproduces F4(90°)=1.7070467.
The cosine series at θ=45° reproduces the tabulated F4(45°)=1.8690931.
The cosine series at θ=120° reproduces the tabulated F4(120°)=1.5439075.

transcription_corrections: The machine transcription of this verso misreads the mirrored recto. Correct readings (from the recto, confirmed by the Fourier check): column 1 at 0° is 2.0863825 (not 0.0863825); column 3 begins 0.2899531, 0.2836165, 0.2826046, ... (not 0.3895931, 0.3836165, ...); column 4 begins 1.9228841, 1.9213942, 1.9169226, ... (not 1.6918841, ...).
The verso is essentially bleed-through from f.28r. The few apparently original ink marks ('5930', '615', '2084', '2') are uncertain and may themselves be recto ink.
